summary: At the CSTO summit in Moscow on 11 November, Putin spoke about the bloc's collective forces, aviation and mobile air-defence units, and Lukashenko called for strengthening the bloc's military capabilities and learning from drone warfare. Neither leader named NATO or the Baltic states in the reports found.
corroboration: Single source (Russian state media), but the statements are on the record.
analysis: Mostly declaratory: the CSTO has rarely acted together. It fits the baseline's picture of Belarus tied ever closer to Russian military planning.

title: Russia offers NATO states 'non-aggression pacts'; Baltic and EU leaders call its security agenda a trap
summary: Russia's chief negotiator says a new European security system was the central topic in Abu Dhabi, and Europeans describe Moscow's demands as limits on NATO enlargement and exercises and a pull-back of forces from the eastern flank. On 12 November Alexei Drobinin, head of foreign-policy planning at Russia's foreign ministry, proposed bilateral agreements with individual NATO members that he said amount to mutual non-aggression pacts. At the Dublin summit Estonia's prime minister Kristen Michal called the talk of security architecture a trap, Lithuania's president Gitanas Nausėda said there must be no spheres of influence and NATO forces must not leave the east, and EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas said the subject can come only after a ceasefire and a peace deal.
corroboration: Russian proposal reported by Militarnyi from a Moscow forum; European reactions reported by Euronews, LRT and UA.NEWS (citing the FT); Lithuania's foreign minister said the same on 10 November.
analysis: This is the part of the Ukraine talks that could directly change Baltic security. Separate pacts with individual members would weaken NATO's collective defence logic, and the Baltic states have the most to lose from any cap on allied forces. For now the US has not endorsed Moscow's agenda and European capitals reject it.

title: After meeting Putin, US envoys say Europeans will join the next round; the Kremlin does not confirm
summary: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Putin in Moscow on 12 November and then Zelensky near Dublin. Witkoff said progress was made, a new trilateral meeting has been set and European representatives will take part. Reuters reports that Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov did not confirm European participation and called Europe's stance a recipe for endless war; Putin said Europe must decide whether it wants peace or war and that Western troops in Ukraine after a deal would lead Russia to resume the war. No date for the next round was given.
corroboration: US account reported by Meduza, TASS and Reuters; the Kremlin side by Reuters; Kyiv Independent confirms the Dublin meeting.
analysis: The two accounts do not match, so European participation should be treated as a US expectation, not an agreement. Putin's line on Western troops is aimed at the European 'coalition of the willing', in which the Baltic states take part.

title: Finland's military says it detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland
summary: A Finnish Defence Forces spokesperson told Reuters that the military detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area on 11 November, is monitoring the situation and sees no immediate military threat to Finland. Ukraine's SBU says it hit the Buyan-M small missile ship Naro-Fominsk, which can carry Kalibr cruise missiles; analysts place the attack near Gogland Island. Estonian media say the ship returned to St Petersburg. Russia has not commented.
corroboration: Finnish statement via Reuters and the Moscow Times; Ukrainian claim via Militarnyi; no imagery of the damage published.
analysis: An independent NATO-country confirmation that a strike took place makes Ukraine's claim much more credible, though the damage is unknown. It shows the war now reaches into the eastern Baltic Sea, close to Finnish and Estonian waters, which raises the risk of stray drones and incidents.

title: FSB says it broke up a Polish spy network in Kaliningrad; Poland calls it disinformation
summary: On 11 November, Poland's Independence Day, the FSB said it had detained two people it described as agents of Poland's military intelligence and internal security agency in Kaliningrad, and warned seven Polish and three Russian citizens. It published a video. A spokesman for Poland's security services, Jacek Dobrzyński, called it a provocation and an act of disinformation, and the foreign ministry urged extreme caution. Polish fact-checkers at OKO.press noted unnatural Polish wording in the published messages and summer foliage in the footage.
corroboration: Reported by Notes from Poland; the FSB material is the only evidence for the claim.
analysis: Neither side's account is independently confirmed. A former Polish security spokesman warns Moscow may use the claim to support its earlier accusation that NATO is preparing to isolate Kaliningrad, a narrative Russia has paired with nuclear warnings since September.

title: Poland indicts a man accused of helping Russia sabotage a railway in 2025
summary: Poland's National Prosecutor's Office said on 12 November it has filed an indictment against a Ukrainian man accused of espionage and sabotage for Russian intelligence. Prosecutors say he scouted the line, chose where explosives would be placed and installed recording devices for the November 2025 attack on the Warsaw–Lublin railway, in which a C4 charge was detonated near Mika. The two main suspects fled to Belarus and are wanted by Interpol.
corroboration: Single official source, reported by Notes from Poland.
analysis: A court has not yet tested the charges. The case fits the pattern in the Lithuanian assessment of Russian services recruiting foreign proxies for disruptive operations, and of Belarus serving as a safe haven.

title: RAND Europe sketches a 2030 Russian attack on Estonia, as a scenario, not a forecast
summary: Meduza reports a RAND Europe study that imagines Putin's death in 2027, a new hard-line leader, a frozen war in Ukraine, and a limited Russian operation in north-east Estonia in 2030 using protests in Narva as a pretext, with NATO invoking Article 5. The authors stress it is one possible path, not a prediction, but say a war in Europe by 2030 is a real risk.
corroboration: Single think-tank report, reported by Meduza.
analysis: Useful as a thinking tool and consistent with the Lithuanian baseline's longer-term warning about limited operations against NATO states, but it is not intelligence and should not be read as evidence of current Russian plans.

title: Bild: Russia's informal plan would take Finland out of NATO and keep NATO bases out of the Baltic states
summary: Germany's Bild reported on 13 November that Russian representatives presented European officials with ideas for a 'new European security order' on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi talks. According to Bild, these include Finland leaving NATO, no NATO military bases in Estonia, Latvia or Lithuania, all of Donbas for Russia, a neutral Ukraine, demilitarised Odesa and Mykolaiv ports and a federal Moldova. In return Russia would withdraw nuclear weapons from Belarus, not deploy intermediate-range missiles there and pull troops out of Transnistria. Bild says this is one of several informal proposals and that it is unclear whether Putin backs it.
corroboration: One report. Interfax-Ukraine, Kyiv Post, Militarnyi, BNN, Meduza, Yle and others all cite Bild, so this is one source, not many. The New York Times and El País describe related Russian papers seeking a NATO pull-back and a veto over exercises, which supports the general direction but not Bild's specific points.
analysis: The general aim, limiting NATO in the east, is well documented on the record; the specific demands are not. Treat them as unconfirmed. If accurate, they would strike at the heart of Baltic security, which is why Baltic and Finnish reactions matter more than the leak itself.

title: Kremlin denies asking Finland to leave NATO; Finland calls the idea outrageous
summary: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a proposal and that it was 'not discussed'; his denial covered Finland, not the other points in Bild's report. Finland's defence minister Antti Häkkänen said demands to reduce NATO's presence near Russia are not negotiable, called the idea outrageous and said Russia is testing US and European resolve by widening its demands beyond Ukraine. Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen said Finland's membership is a matter for Finland and NATO alone.
corroboration: Peskov's denial is reported by Meduza, Kyiv Post and Türkiye Today; Häkkänen's remarks by Bloomberg (via UNITED24 and Censor.net). No Baltic government statement on the Bild report itself was found.
analysis: A narrow denial on Finland leaves the Baltic part of the report unanswered. Finland's response matches what Lithuania's president said on 12 November: no spheres of influence and no repeat of Russia's 2021 demands.

title: Moscow sets a condition for European participation, contradicting the US account
summary: US envoys said after meeting Putin on 12 November that Europeans would join the next round of talks. On 13 November Peskov said Europe must first show 'genuine' readiness to contribute to peace and that no decision on a wider format had been taken. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas replied that Russia does not decide who represents the EU. Latvia's prime minister Andris Kulbergs called the process 'not real peace talks' and said Russia is in no position to make demands.
corroboration: Reuters (via The Moscow Times) for Peskov and Kallas; LSM for Kulbergs. Ukraine's president also says Europe will take part as an equal participant.
analysis: The US and Russia are giving incompatible accounts. Moscow appears to use access to the table as leverage over Europe, which fits the Russian narrative, tracked by EUvsDisinfo, that Europe is the obstacle to peace.

title: Gulf of Finland strike: Russia stays silent as Finland raises concerns with Kyiv
summary: Russia has still not commented on the 11 November strike that Ukraine's SBU says hit the Buyan-M missile ship Naro-Fominsk near Gogland (Suursaari). Estonian media say the vessel returned to St Petersburg. The same night, drones damaged fuel tanks at the Ust-Luga port, injuring three workers according to the regional governor. Finland's defence minister said Helsinki raised the strike with Kyiv because of the narrow gulf's sensitivity for shipping and the environment, while stressing that the sea around Finland is safe.
corroboration: Al Jazeera, Yle and Defense News; Finland's detection is independent of Ukraine's claim.
analysis: The Baltic Fleet is being hit, not freed up, which is consistent with the baseline. The risk to watch is spillover: stray drones and Russian accusations that Baltic states or Finland help Ukraine, which Lithuania has already called false.

title: Fact-checkers map Russian messages around the talks; Poland braces for a sabotage-anniversary campaign
summary: EUvsDisinfo, republished by StopFake on 13 November, lists the main pro-Kremlin lines around the Abu Dhabi talks: Europe is the warmonger and the obstacle to peace, Western peacekeepers would be occupiers, and the US should cut a deal without Europe. A Warsaw security firm rates disinformation risk in Poland as high and expects the 16 November anniversary of the 2025 rail sabotage to be used to blame Ukrainians. Lithuania's crisis management chief said on 11 November that online claims that Lithuania let Ukrainian drones through its airspace are completely false.
corroboration: EUvsDisinfo/StopFake (EU-funded and Ukrainian fact-checkers), Global Security Centre (commercial), Lithuanian official via European Pravda.
analysis: These are forecasts and narrative maps, not incidents. They are useful for readers: the same messages are aimed at the Baltic states, especially after any drone or sabotage event.

title: Russian state media keeps a running count of NATO surveillance flights near Kaliningrad
summary: TASS reports, citing an unnamed air-traffic source, that a US-registered NATO reconnaissance aircraft spent five hours near the Kaliningrad region on 13 November, its third such flight this week and more than 70 this year, flying over Polish and Lithuanian airspace and international waters.
corroboration: Single anonymous source in Russian state media; flight-tracking of such aircraft is public, and the flights stay outside Russian airspace.
analysis: Routine reconnaissance is not a provocation, but the steady reporting feeds Moscow's story that NATO is preparing to isolate Kaliningrad, which this briefing rates as unsupported.

title: Leaked Russian paper: NATO back to 1997, no British or French nuclear umbrella for Europe
summary: The New York Times reported on 13 November that Russian officials circulated an unsigned 'non-paper' dated 10 November at the Abu Dhabi talks. According to the NYT and outlets summarising it, it asks NATO to pull troops and bases back to 1997 positions, give up further enlargement and any military activity in Ukraine, Eastern Europe, the South Caucasus and Central Asia, end Western arms supplies to Ukraine, keep Ukraine out of the EU's common defence policy, and asks Britain and France not to use their nuclear weapons to protect other European states. The Telegraph on 14 November described a paper with the same date and highlighted the demand on Britain's deterrent.
corroboration: The NYT says it obtained a copy from a negotiator and a second source confirmed it is authentic; The Telegraph's account matches. The paper itself has not been published, and the Kremlin has not commented.
analysis: Every Baltic state, Poland and Finland joined NATO after 1997, so this is a demand to remove allied forces from them. It is the most concrete evidence yet that Moscow links a Ukraine deal to rolling back Baltic security, as the Lithuanian assessment warns. It is still an opening position in talks, not an action.

title: US, Finnish and European leaders reject the 1997 demand
summary: US Senate intelligence committee chairman Tom Cotton called the idea of NATO members withdrawing from their own territory preposterous. A US official told reporters that the envoys reminded Moscow how much has changed since its 2021 demands. Finland's defence minister said the demands test US and European resolve. In Dublin, 43 European Political Community countries signed a declaration that European security is for Europeans to decide, and the UK prime minister said the same after the meeting.
corroboration: Ukrinform (Cotton and the US official, citing the NYT), Euronews (EPC declaration), Euromaidan Press (UK reaction).
analysis: Western rejection is broad and on the record. Accounts differ on Europe's seat: Bloomberg, via ISW, says five countries plus an EU representative were named for technical talks, while Euronews reports no agreement yet on an EU envoy, and Russia has not said it accepts them.

title: Estonia: Russian missile ship hit several times, with dead and wounded
summary: At a defence ministry briefing on 13 November, an Estonian Defence Forces colonel said more than three Ukrainian drones hit the Baltic Fleet corvette Naro-Fominsk on 11 November, causing deaths and injuries, and that it could not continue under its own power and was escorted toward St Petersburg. He said the same night's strike on Ust-Luga cut the port's oil throughput from about 700,000 to about 300,000 tonnes a day, and that a Russian helicopter was destroyed by its own air defence.
corroboration: ERR, Kyiv Post and others report the same briefing; Ukraine's SBU made the original claim; Russia has still not commented.
analysis: An independent NATO-country military now confirms the strike, so the claim moves to confirmed. The Baltic Fleet is losing ships and attention to Ukrainian attacks, which is the opposite of forces being freed for the Baltic direction.

title: Moscow and Minsk: NATO is the threat, we are not preparing for war
summary: Foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told TASS on 14 November that NATO undermines Europe's security like 'a bad tooth' and that Europe would be safer without it, replying to Germany's chancellor. On 11 November Belarusian state TV quoted Lukashenko telling a CSTO meeting that Belarus and Russia are not preparing for war with NATO or the EU by 2030 and accusing Europe of militarising.
corroboration: Russian and Belarusian state media; no independent reporting needed for the fact that they said it.
analysis: Both lines serve the same goal as the leaked paper: to present NATO's eastern presence as the problem. Denials of intent cannot be tested; the baseline judges that Russia is rebuilding capacity for possible limited operations in the longer term, regardless of what it says now.

title: Poland plans to extend its closed zone on the Belarus border
summary: Poland's interior ministry has drafted a regulation to extend the temporary ban on entering a strip along 78 km of the Belarus border for 90 days, from 30 November to 27 February 2027. It counts 482 attempted illegal crossings this year up to 8 November, calls the migration pressure artificially created by Belarus, and notes more balloons and drones from Belarus, mostly for smuggling, without ruling out destabilisation.
corroboration: Defence24 reporting on the draft regulation.
analysis: A steady, managed pressure rather than a new escalation. It matches the Baltic experience with balloons from Belarus and the baseline's description of hybrid pressure from Minsk.

title: Commentators claim Ukraine is deliberately routing drones through NATO airspace
summary: Pro-Kremlin and contrarian commentators, including a widely read Substack blog, argue that Ukraine deliberately sends drones through Polish and Baltic airspace to avoid Russian air defences, and repeat an unverified claim that a balloon from the Baltics delivered a bomb used in an attack in St Petersburg. Estonia's foreign minister says no state has been authorised to fly drones through Estonian airspace; Estonia's defence minister says most drones stayed in Russian airspace.
corroboration: No official, investigative or imagery-based source supports deliberate routing or the balloon claim.
analysis: Stray drones, likely knocked off course by Russian electronic warfare according to Lithuania's defence minister, are a real safety problem, but intent has not been shown. The narrative helps Moscow cast the Baltic states as co-belligerents.

title: Estonia foils GRU-linked arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems
summary: Shortly after 3 a.m. on 14 November, attackers tried to break into the Threod Systems building in Viimsi, north of Tallinn, and pour in flammable liquid to cause a fire and explosion. The company's security team stopped them; no one was hurt and production was not affected. Estonia's security police and border guard detained eight residents of Latvia, and prosecutors asked a court to arrest five. KAPO's director general said counterintelligence had confirmed that Russia's GRU coordinated the attack, and that the GRU recruits EU residents from criminal circles or in financial difficulty because they can move freely in the Schengen area.
corroboration: ERR, LSM, Ukrainian and international media report the same official account; Latvia's VDD separately confirms its role and the searches in Latvia.
analysis: This is well supported on the facts: a physical attack, eight detentions and seizures in two countries. The GRU attribution comes from intelligence that has not been published, so it is a strong official judgement rather than a proven fact. It follows the August arson at Milrem Robotics, also blamed on Russia, and fits the baseline's warning about proxy sabotage against firms that supply Ukraine.

title: Latvia's security service tipped off Estonia and found explosives at home
summary: Latvia's State Security Service (VDD) says it received information about possible sabotage in Estonia and passed it to KAPO, after which both services acted together. On 14 November VDD searched nine sites in Latvia linked to the suspects and seized explosive devices, pyrotechnics, ammunition and many phones and storage devices. VDD said Russian-organised sabotage aims to raise tension and fear and to slow support for Ukraine.
corroboration: LSM report on the VDD press release; KAPO publicly credited Latvian help.
analysis: A second, independent national service backs the Estonian account, which makes the case stronger than a single-country attribution. The use of Latvian residents again shows Russia hiring people from neighbouring EU states rather than sending its own officers.

title: Estonia to close road border crossings with Russia on 1 December
summary: Prime Minister Kristen Michal asked the interior minister and the Government Office to prepare to close the border, saying Estonia must reduce risks if Russia continues hybrid attacks. The foreign ministry says the Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula road crossings will close to pedestrians and vehicles on 1 December; residents in Russia have two weeks to return. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. The government will decide in the coming days whether the closure is temporary or indefinite.
corroboration: ERR, TASS, The Irish Times (wire report) and ISW report the decision; the exact legal decision is still pending.
analysis: A significant political step, following Finland's earlier full closure. It will mostly affect cross-border families and trade around Narva and gives Moscow material for a 'Russophobia' narrative, but it does not change the military picture.

title: Kremlin: talks on European security pointless if Europe does not want peace
summary: On 15 November Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said discussing European security makes no sense unless Europeans really want peace, and that without prospects of agreement Russia would have to use force to reach its goals. He added that Europe's negotiators had not yet contacted Moscow. Separately, foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Russia would check reports of Estonia's border plans and called them, if true, aggressive Russophobia. On 13 November Peskov had said that no withdrawal of current NATO members was discussed at the Abu Dhabi talks.
corroboration: TASS reports both statements; Western media summarise them.
analysis: The force remark is a general statement about Russia's war aims, not a new explicit threat against NATO. Peskov's denial that NATO withdrawals were discussed sits uneasily with the leaked 10 November paper, described by the NYT and The Telegraph, that asks NATO to return to 1997 positions; a pull-back of forces is not the same as members leaving, so both can be technically true.

title: Finland: Russian pull-back demands are not negotiable
summary: Finland's defence minister Antti Häkkänen called the reported Russian demands for less NATO presence near its borders outrageous and not negotiable, and a test of US and European resolve. Bild's report that Moscow wants Finland to leave NATO is still denied by the Kremlin and is not in the accounts of the leaked paper.
corroboration: Bloomberg, UPI and Meduza report the Finnish response.
analysis: Helsinki's rejection is firm and on the record. The narrower Finland-exit claim remains contested; the broader 1997 demand, which would also cover the Baltic states, is better supported.

title: Drones hit ships in Romanian waters, including a NATO-flagged tanker
summary: According to ISW, unidentified and possibly Russian drones struck four commercial vessels in Romanian waters between 13 and 15 November, three of them near Sulina, and Romania scrambled fighter jets twice. ISW says the Greek-flagged tanker Evia Petrol V is the first ship flying a NATO member's flag to be hit; Russian milbloggers claimed the ships carried cargo for Ukraine.
corroboration: ISW summary of Romanian official statements; the attacker has not been officially named.
analysis: Outside the Baltic region, but relevant: it shows Russia's war spilling into NATO waters in ways that stay below the threshold of an attack on an ally, the same grey-zone pattern seen with drones over the Baltic states.

title: Poland marks a year since the rail sabotage amid disinformation
summary: 16 November is the first anniversary of the 2025 explosions on the Warsaw–Lublin line, which Poland blamed on Russian services; the state rail accident commission has confirmed both attacks were terrorist in nature. A Polish security consultancy reports disinformation claiming the state cannot protect citizens, and a wave of pro-UPA graffiti on monuments in several cities that may be paid work designed to stir anti-Ukrainian feeling; a 17-year-old Ukrainian was detained in the Tri-City area.
corroboration: Single commercial monitor (Global Security Centre); the commission findings and the detention are official.
analysis: The vandalism has not been attributed to Russia by Polish authorities, so it should not be counted as sabotage. It fits a known tactic of hiring people online for provocations, but that link is unproven.

title: Kremlin calls Estonia's GRU accusation baseless
summary: On 16 November Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow rejects Estonia's claim that Russian military intelligence ordered the attempted arson at Threod Systems, calling it entirely baseless. He described Estonia's planned border closure as building a wall and said walls have never done their builders any good. A day earlier the foreign ministry spokeswoman said Russia would check the reports and would see a closure as Russophobia.
corroboration: Reported by the Moscow Times, Meduza, RT and TASS; the wording matches across Russian state and independent outlets.
analysis: This sets up a direct contradiction: Estonia says it has clear evidence, Russia says there is none. Moscow offers no alternative explanation for the detentions and seized materials, and it has denied every earlier European sabotage attribution, including cases later proven in court. The denial does not weaken the Estonian case, but the evidence on both sides remains unpublished.

title: Threod case: suspects held, Estonia presses Latvia
summary: Estonian prosecutors asked a court to remand five of the eight residents of Latvia detained over the 14 November arson attempt; Meduza reports five have been arrested. The prosecutor general said investigators now want to establish how the attack was organised and who else was involved. In an interview with ERR, the head of Estonia's security police thanked Latvian colleagues but said he hoped Latvia would take sufficient measures, implying that a full Estonian border closure might make it sensible for Latvia to follow.
corroboration: RTE and LSM report the same official account; Meduza adds the arrest figure.
analysis: The investigation is moving through the courts, which is the right test of the GRU attribution. The remarks about Latvia point to a quiet strain among the Baltic states over how to stop proxies recruited in one country from attacking in another.

title: Lithuania's president: closing the Russian border is an option
summary: On 16 November President Gitanas Nausėda called Estonia's decision appropriate and said Lithuania could take similar steps if attempts to destabilise the region continue. He said Lithuania must weigh its role as the transit country to Kaliningrad, and argued that Russia does not understand when its actions get no response.
corroboration: LRT and European Pravda report the same remarks.
analysis: This is a conditional statement, not a decision. Closing Lithuania's border would collide with the 2002 EU–Russia arrangement on Kaliningrad transit, which Moscow treats as highly sensitive, so any real move would raise tension far more than Estonia's closure.

title: Two US Army battalions arrive in Lithuania
summary: A heavy battalion and an engineer battalion of the US 1st Infantry Division were welcomed at the Pabradė training area on 16 November. The engineers will help with obstacle building and the Baltic Defence Line. Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas called the US presence an important deterrent, and Lithuania has submitted a proposal to Washington for a permanent US base.
corroboration: LRT, based on Lithuanian defence ministry information.
analysis: After a summer when only about 100 US troops remained in Lithuania during a US force review, this restores the rotational presence announced in September. It is a planned allied deployment, not a response to a new Russian move.

title: Estonia's closure: who it hits, and plans to run the state from abroad
summary: Estonia's three road crossings handle 1,300–1,800 people a day and are among the last land routes between Russia and the EU. Yle reports that Russians living in Finland will lose their quickest route home, and Narva businesses expect to lose trade. The cabinet will decide this week whether the closure is temporary or indefinite. Separately, Politico reports that Estonia plans to move state digital services to cloud storage abroad so they keep running if the country is occupied or data centres are destroyed.
corroboration: Meduza summarises Estonian officials, Yle and Politico; Daily Northern summarises Yle.
analysis: Some headlines present the cloud plan as a doomsday plan; it extends Estonia's long-standing data embassy in Luxembourg and is contingency planning, not a sign of an expected invasion. The social cost of the closure falls largely on Russian-speaking residents, which Moscow is likely to use in its messaging.

title: EU adds sanctions and boards a falsely flagged tanker
summary: EU foreign ministers agreed 113 new sanctions listings on 16 November aimed at the money behind Russia's war. EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas said the EU naval mission IRINI had boarded the tanker MV MIDAG in the Mediterranean on 13 November and confirmed it was sailing under a false flag, and that the EU will keep disrupting Russia's shadow fleet.
corroboration: TheJournal.ie and Euromaidan Press report the listings and the boarding; Militarnyi and others repeat the same EU statement.
analysis: The boarding happened outside the Baltic, but it matters there: the baseline links shadow-fleet ships to damage to undersea infrastructure, and Russia warned on 10 November of retaliatory ship seizures if the EU stops its tankers. Watch for Russian naval escorts in the Baltic Sea in response.

title: Coordinated Russian campaign over Estonia's Soviet memorials
summary: Estonia's Propastop says that between 10 and 14 November Russia's chargé d'affaires in Tallinn told RIA Novosti that at least 140 Soviet war memorials had been destroyed in Estonia, and RIA, Izvestia, RT and other outlets repeated it in near-identical wording, with Telegram channels adding outrage. Estonia's government catalogued 322 Soviet monuments, of which 244 were marked for removal or replacement; war graves are kept.
corroboration: One Estonian monitor's analysis; the identical wording across Russian outlets is visible in its examples.
analysis: The pattern of diplomats setting the line, agencies spreading it and Telegram amplifying it is a textbook example of the information operations the Lithuanian assessment describes. It also lands just as Moscow seeks to portray Estonia's border closure as hostility toward Russians.

title: Estonia's president: border closure cannot be an emotional decision
summary: On 17 November President Ülle Madise said the decision to close Estonia's road crossings with Russia should rest on an analysis of its economic, humanitarian, diplomatic and security effects, and said a closure would not have prevented the attacks on Milrem Robotics or Threod Systems. She favoured stopping ordinary tourist and shopping trips while keeping diplomatic and humanitarian travel. The foreign minister had announced a closure from 1 December, and the prime minister told Delfi it should be indefinite; the cabinet has not yet formally decided.
corroboration: ERR and Meduza report the president's remarks; TASS reported the prime minister's interview.
analysis: This is a debate about whether the measure fits the threat, not about who is behind the attacks: the Threod suspects were residents of Latvia recruited at a distance, so a road closure would not have stopped them, although it would cut travel that the baseline links to recruitment and sanctions evasion. Expect Russian outlets to present the debate as a split in Tallinn.

title: Estonian parties split on checks at the Latvian border
summary: The Centre Party and EKRE want checks restored on Estonia's border with Latvia, citing saboteurs and illegal migrants who came through Latvia; Isamaa is open to them if other measures fail. Reform, the Social Democrats and Eesti 200 oppose the idea. Interior Minister Igor Taro said the government is far from considering it and estimated the cost at about 300 million euros.
corroboration: ERR, based on party leaders' statements.
analysis: The debate follows the security police chief's public hope that Latvia will take sufficient measures. It shows strain among the Baltic states over threats that move freely inside Schengen, but no government is proposing checks for now.

title: Estonian security police: about ten defence firms are Russian targets
summary: In an ERR interview, Estonia's security police chief Margo Palloson said Russia is targeting about ten Estonian defence industry companies, including Threod Systems, that Estonia had information about the planned Threod attack in advance, and that Russian services recruit through criminal networks, social media and people travelling to Russia, sometimes paying only a few hundred euros.
corroboration: ERR interview, summarised by United24; consistent with the Lithuanian and Estonian assessments of proxy sabotage.
analysis: This explains why Estonia treats the Threod case as part of a campaign rather than a one-off. It is an official assessment without published evidence, but it is consistent with the earlier, formally attributed Milrem arson in August.

title: Belarus orders snap readiness check of border-guard units
summary: On 16 November Belarus's Security Council secretary announced a snap combat-readiness inspection of State Border Committee units, focused on rapid-response groups. The drills include marches and repelling simulated sabotage and reconnaissance groups, with results reported to Alexander Lukashenko. No location or duration was given.
corroboration: Kyiv Independent, citing the Belarusian state agency Belta; ISW reported nothing significant in Belarus the next day.
analysis: Snap inspections of this kind are common in Belarus and this one involves border guards, not army units. It is worth watching because Belarusian border structures are suspected of helping organise migrant crossings, but there is no reported movement toward NATO borders.

title: Lavrov restates 2021 demands; Rutte says Putin wants to weaken Europe
summary: On 17 November Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused European officials of trying to squeeze into negotiations to build a European security system aimed at Russia and said Moscow remains committed to its 2021 demands on NATO; deputy minister Sergei Ryabkov said there is no discussion of European participation in talks. The same day NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte told the Ukraine Defense Contact Group that Putin aims to weaken Europe by generating insecurity and sowing division.
corroboration: ISW's 17 November assessment summarises the Russian statements; Kyiv Post reports Rutte's remarks.
analysis: The 2021 demands included pulling NATO forces back from member states that joined after 1997, which covers the Baltic states, so the statement matches the leaked paper reported last week. ISW notes it contradicts US envoys' proposals. It reveals long-term aims, not military preparation.

title: Lithuanian army chief: US troops a relief, drone defence still a gap
summary: Lithuania's armed forces commander Raimundas Vaikšnoras said the arrival of the two US battalions brought relief and that he expects more than a one-off rotation. He said radar coverage has improved but identifying and neutralising drones, especially at night, remains a gap until Lithuania acquires its own capabilities.
corroboration: LRT interview.
analysis: A frank admission that matches the November drone alerts, when NATO jets could not shoot down a drone. It points to air defence as the main near-term vulnerability, which fits the hybrid rather than conventional threat picture.

title: Polish paper: Russia planned a mass-casualty false flag near Kaliningrad
summary: Rzeczpospolita reported on 17–18 November, citing anonymous senior sources close to Poland's military and security services, that Russian intelligence planned a sabotage operation near the Polish–Kaliningrad border in late October or early November that was meant to cause many casualties and be blamed on Ukraine. Allied intelligence reportedly warned Warsaw, and the Baltic states got similar warnings. Poland responded with extra police, border guards and security officers and a special operations headquarters. Special-services coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak would not confirm the plot but said the measures were taken because the threat was judged real.
corroboration: Repeated by The Telegraph, European Pravda, Kyiv Post, Meduza and TVP World, all relying on the same newspaper; no second independent source.
analysis: This may explain the early-November alert that Prime Minister Tusk announced on 3 November, but the core claim is still unconfirmed and the retellings already disagree on where the attack would have happened and who the victims would have been. A one-source story picked up widely should not be treated as several confirmations.

title: Russia reportedly offers to thin Kaliningrad and Belarus forces in exchange for a NATO rollback
summary: Bloomberg and the New York Times reported on 18 November, citing sources and a document, that Russia's negotiating position asks NATO to return to its 1997 military footprint, stop treating Russia as a threat and set up incident-prevention mechanisms in the Baltic and Black Seas; in return Moscow would reduce its military presence in Kaliningrad and Belarus. US envoys reportedly put the idea to European allies. They are due at a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin on 19 November hosted by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
corroboration: Two major outlets report the document; Meduza and Kyiv Post summarise them. No official confirmation.
analysis: A 1997 footprint would mean removing allied forces from the Baltic states, Poland and Finland, so for the Baltic region this is the 2021 demand with a sweetener attached. The offer is vague and would leave Russia's own forces next door, which is why European governments have rejected the idea so far.

title: Ukrainian intelligence: attack on the Baltics unlikely, but Russia is building depots
summary: Presenting a report on Russian information pressure in Kyiv on 18 November, Yevhen Yerin of Ukraine's military intelligence said direct Russian aggression against the Baltic states or Poland is unlikely because Moscow remains focused on Ukraine. He warned of possible provocations against military or logistics sites to test how fast NATO reacts, and said Russia is setting up ammunition and fuel depots and communication hubs in Kaliningrad, Belarus and western Russia, with more operational-tactical missile systems in Belarus.
corroboration: Reported by Interfax-Ukraine and UA.News; no supporting imagery or details published.
analysis: The overall judgement matches Lithuania's baseline and Finnish and Baltic officials' statements. The depot claim is new and worth watching, but it comes without evidence from a party to the war.

title: Estonian parliament backs border-closure bill; Latvian border checks would cost €65 million
summary: On 18 November Estonia's parliament passed an opposition Isamaa bill to close all crossing points with Russia in first reading, 37 to 2, while the government prepares the closure announced for 1 December. The same day, Interior Ministry secretary general Tarmo Miilits estimated that restoring checks on the Latvian border would cost about €65 million, said there is no security need for them now and argued the money would do more as extra police patrols and counterintelligence. He said agencies are ready for possible Russian retaliation through illegal migration.
corroboration: Reported by ERR, LSM, APA and TASS; TASS stresses the objections of Narva's mayor and council.
analysis: The vote shows broad political support for the closure despite the president's call for an impact analysis. The €65 million figure differs from the roughly €300 million cited in Estonian debate earlier this week; neither article says what period the costs cover.

title: Lithuania keeps troops on the Kaliningrad border; army chief suggests barriers
summary: Lithuania has extended army help to its border guards on the Kaliningrad border to the end of November, with about 100 soldiers patrolling near checkpoints since 8 October. Chief of Defence Raimundas Vaikšnoras said on 17 November that constant patrols are costly and proposed physical barriers on the most vulnerable sections, like those on the Belarus border. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas calls the deployment preventive, prompted by public reports of a possible Russian mobilisation rather than intelligence, and officials say the threat level has not risen.
corroboration: Reported by LRT/BNS and Reform.news (Elta).
analysis: A precaution against sabotage, draft evasion and smuggling, not a response to Russian military moves; it fits the cautious, hybrid-focused posture of the baseline.

title: Estonia presses for more US troops as Bloomberg reports smaller cuts than feared
summary: Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said on 17 November that NATO's eastern flank needs a larger American presence and that Washington's decision on its forces in Europe should be clear by early winter. Bloomberg has reported that US troop cuts in Europe will be smaller than feared, falling mainly on Germany. Estonian parliamentary committee chairs expect no major cuts in the region, pointing to new US rotations in Estonia and Lithuania.
corroboration: Reported by ERR; the Bloomberg report on cuts is not independently confirmed.
analysis: Allied force levels matter for deterrence in the baseline's longer-term scenario. For now the trend in the Baltic states is toward more, not fewer, US troops on the ground.

title: Lithuania plans fencing on parts of the Kaliningrad border
summary: Lithuania's State Border Guard Service presented Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas with a plan to reinforce the border with Russia's Kaliningrad region, including a segmented barbed-wire fence on selected stretches. The minister said more money is needed and that measures from the Belarus border cannot simply be copied, because much of this border runs along the Neman river, the Curonian Spit and the sea. Army commander Raimundas Vaikšnoras had earlier suggested barriers on the most vulnerable sections, and soldiers are helping border guards until the end of November.
corroboration: Reported by LRT and European Pravda from the same ministry briefing; one source.
analysis: This is a defensive step driven by recent hybrid incidents and a possible Russian mobilisation after the Duma elections, not by any reported Russian build-up; officials themselves say the threat level has not risen. Expect Russian media to present it as provocation.

title: Russian envoy warns of strategic-forces response to Lithuanian and Polish nuclear debate
summary: At the OSCE security forum in Vienna on 18 November, the head of Russia's delegation said Russia's strategic deterrence forces would take response measures if Lithuania and Poland lift their bans on hosting nuclear weapons. She said NATO is weighing more troops and nuclear deployments in both countries and complained of growing reconnaissance near Kaliningrad. Lithuania passed the first of three parliamentary votes to remove its constitutional ban on 6 October; the final vote is expected in January.
corroboration: Reported by TASS; Russian embassies made similar Kaliningrad-related nuclear threats in late September.
analysis: A conditional warning in a diplomatic forum, not a new policy. The claim that NATO is assessing nuclear deployments in Lithuania and Poland is not backed by any NATO decision; Lithuania's debate concerns removing a legal ban, not a request for weapons.

title: Ukraine's foreign ministry says Russia is building a pretext against NATO's eastern flank
summary: Ukraine's foreign ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi said on 18 November, presenting a study by Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation, that Russia is running an information campaign that could prepare the ground for aggression against NATO's eastern flank, while stressing that no one knows whether an attack will happen. A military intelligence spokesman said at the same event that Russia is strengthening logistics near NATO borders and in Belarus.
corroboration: Reported by Censor.net and UA.News from the same event; no primary data or imagery was shown.
analysis: Ukraine has an interest in keeping Western attention on the Russian threat. The warning is about information pressure and long-term risk; it sits alongside Ukraine's own military intelligence judging a direct attack unlikely while the war continues, and the Baltic baseline says the same.

title: Estonia's prime minister: Russia's security talks would make the Baltics bargaining chips
summary: Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote in The Economist that engaging Moscow's demand for talks on Europe's security architecture risks turning the Baltic states and Poland into bargaining chips and creating a two-tier NATO. He said the existing rules, from the Helsinki Final Act to the Paris Charter, already work and that Russia broke them. He urged continued support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia.
corroboration: Reported by ERR; consistent with Michal's statements at the Dublin European Council on 13 November.
analysis: This is a political position, not new intelligence, but it shows the Baltic governments' main worry: that Russia's demand for a NATO rollback to 1997 could be traded in peace talks. Reported Russian offers to thin forces in Kaliningrad and Belarus are part of the same bargaining.

title: Poll: most Lithuanians think Russia could attack, fewer trust allies to defend
summary: A Norstat poll for the agency Bosanova, presented on 19 November, found 62% of Lithuanians believe Russia could attack the Baltic states, slightly down from last year, and 56% worry about a Russian provocation. Only 48% believe NATO allies could defend Lithuania; trust was 68% in the German brigade and 43% in US forces. 29% want the war in Ukraine to end quickly even at the cost of Ukrainian land.
corroboration: Reported by LRT; margin of error about 3 points.
analysis: A public-opinion measure, not a threat indicator. The gap between fear of attack and trust in allies is the kind of doubt Russian information operations seek to widen, as the baseline notes.

title: No confirmation yet of the reported Kaliningrad false-flag plot
summary: No government has confirmed Rzeczpospolita's report that Russian intelligence planned a mass-casualty attack near the Polish–Kaliningrad border to blame on Ukraine. ISW notes that Poland's police chief said on 2 November the special operation followed warnings of possible sabotage on that border in the first half of November, and that the operation was extended to 15 November.
corroboration: ISW's summary relies on the same newspaper plus earlier on-record Polish statements about the alert itself.
analysis: The on-record statements confirm an alert and a real threat assessment, not the specific false-flag plan. The claim stays unconfirmed.

title: Russian missiles and a drone come down in eastern Poland
summary: During one of the largest Russian strikes on Ukraine of the war, two Russian missiles and a probable jet-powered drone landed in south-eastern Poland early on 20 November, near Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik nad Sanem and Mołodycz. Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz identified one as a Kh-101 cruise missile and said the date was not chosen by chance, since a Coalition of the Willing exercise was under way nearby. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it an intentional provocation. No casualties or damage to critical infrastructure were reported, and nothing was shot down.
corroboration: Reported by Reuters (via the Moscow Times), AP (via PBS and the Manila Times), the Kyiv Independent, Newsweek and UNITED24; early local reports spoke of two objects before the minister confirmed three.
analysis: The facts are well established; the intent is not. Debris landing tens of kilometres from the Ukrainian border during a strike on western Ukraine fits spillover, a pattern seen before, while Poland's reading of deliberate timing is a judgement it has not yet backed with published evidence. Either way, it shows the risk to NATO territory from Russia's air campaign.

title: NATO calls it a grave violation; Poland seeks more allied support
summary: NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte called the landings a grave violation of Polish airspace and clearly dangerous, and is expected to visit Poland this weekend. Kosiniak-Kamysz said Poland will ask NATO for more support on the eastern flank. No request for Article 4 consultations had been reported by the time of writing, unlike after the drone incursion last year.
corroboration: Rutte's statement carried by AP; the support request reported by Reuters.
analysis: The response so far is political and defensive. Whether Poland asks for formal consultations, and what extra air defence allies offer, is the next thing to watch; Baltic air defence gaps were exposed by the drone that NATO jets twice failed to bring down over Lithuania on 10–11 November.

title: Trump says Putin sent 'little missiles' into Poland by mistake
summary: In a Fox News interview given on Air Force One on 19 November, after a three-way meeting with Putin and Xi Jinping in China, Trump said Putin had been landing drones and a couple of small missiles in Poland by mistake. He was responding to criticism from Tusk after calling Putin his friend. The remarks came hours before the new missile landings, though some outlets presented them as a reaction to it.
corroboration: Reported by Meduza, Hromadske, Ukrinform and Newsweek; Hromadske gives the date and setting, others do not.
analysis: The remark concerns earlier incursions, not Friday's missiles, so reports framing it as Trump's verdict on the new incident run ahead of the facts. It still shows a gap between Washington's tone and Warsaw's, which Moscow can exploit.

title: Estonia approves border closure; Moscow promises a response
summary: Estonia's government formally approved closing all five road checkpoints with Russia from 1 December, with a review after six months; rail is unaffected. It cites the 14 November arson attempt at drone maker Threod Systems near Tallinn, which it says Russian military intelligence ordered; eight people from Latvia were detained. Foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Estonia is building a new Iron Curtain and Russia would take political and diplomatic measures. Estonia's president urged the cabinet not to act on emotion.
corroboration: Reported by Euronews and Reuters (via the Moscow Times); the GRU attribution rests on Estonia's security service.
analysis: The Russian response is limited to diplomacy for now. Estonia's own debate, including the president's caution and concerns from the Setomaa border community, shows the closure is contested at home, which Russian media are amplifying, as the monitor Propastop documents.

title: Trump–Xi–Putin meeting ends without a deal on Ukraine
summary: The three leaders met in China on 19 November. Reports say the meeting ended with a general peace declaration that did not mention Ukraine and no major agreement. Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov said separately that inviting French, German and British representatives to Moscow does not mean Russia accepts their role in US-brokered talks.
corroboration: Reported by Axios, Euronews and AP.
analysis: No sign of a settlement that would free Russian forces from Ukraine, which is the main trigger the baseline would watch for. The reported Russian demand for a NATO rollback toward its 1997 footprint remains on the table.

title: Drones hit Russian military supply ship in the Gulf of Finland
summary: On the morning of 21 November two drones struck the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, sailing from St Petersburg to Kaliningrad. The ship caught fire and drifted into Finnish territorial waters, where Finland's Border Guard led the rescue. The vessel belongs to a company that serves Russia's defence ministry and is under US sanctions. Finland's Defence Forces said Ukraine is quite possibly behind the attack, and Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said Ukraine has the right to fight back. Finland twice restricted sea and air traffic as a precaution.
corroboration: Reported by ERR, Reuters (via the Moscow Times), Al Jazeera, TASS and ISW. Accounts of the location differ: Russia says neutral waters 3 nautical miles from its border, Estonia's police an international lane north of Vaindloo, Finland's defence ministry international waters. Russian accounts of the crew differ too, from evacuation under way to evacuation not needed.
analysis: No one has claimed the strike, so attribution to Ukraine remains a judgement. For the Baltic states the risk is spillover: drones and fires in the busy shipping lane between Finland and Estonia, and a Russian argument that the Kaliningrad sea route is under threat, which Moscow could use to justify naval escorts.

title: Rutte in Warsaw: NATO will defend every inch of Poland
summary: NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte met Prime Minister Donald Tusk in Warsaw on 21 November, said all allies stand in full solidarity with Poland and called the airspace breach dangerous and unacceptable. Poland asked for more support under NATO's Eastern Sentry mission, including surveillance aircraft and F-35 fighters, but did not request Article 4 consultations. Military prosecutors in Lublin are investigating all three objects.
corroboration: Reported by Anadolu (citing TVP Info), Reuters and the Warsaw-based Global Security Centre.
analysis: The response remains defensive and political. Poland choosing not to invoke Article 4, unlike after the 2025 drone incursion, suggests Warsaw wants more air defence rather than a formal crisis.

title: Kremlin denies violating Polish airspace; Russian media twist Sikorski's words
summary: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the claims of Russian airspace violations empty and groundless. Sputnik reported that Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski had admitted Warsaw lacks proof the missiles were Russian; what he said was that Poland is waiting for confirmation of concrete facts. Poland's defence minister has identified one object as a Kh-101, a missile only Russia uses.
corroboration: Peskov's denial and Sikorski's remark are carried by Sputnik, a Russian state outlet; the defence minister's identification is reported by Polish media via Gwara Media and the Kyiv Independent.
analysis: The Russian framing turns normal caution during an investigation into a supposed admission. It is the same pattern fact-checkers documented after the 2025 drone incursion.

title: Air alerts and unverified explosions around Baltiysk
summary: On the evening of 21 November air raid sirens sounded across parts of the Kaliningrad region, and Russian accounts reported explosions and drones near the Baltic Fleet base at Baltiysk. Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh said an alert in the Neman district followed a suspicious aerial object approaching from Lithuania and that specialists found no threat. There was no official confirmation of a strike, damage or casualties.
corroboration: Reported by the Kyiv Independent, which could not verify the explosions; no Lithuanian comment was found.
analysis: Treat with caution. The claim that an object came from Lithuania fits a Russian narrative that the Baltic states help Ukraine strike Russia; no evidence has been published to support it.

title: Moscow says it will not attack NATO, and that NATO wants war
summary: At her weekly briefing on 20 November, foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Russia has no intention of attacking NATO member states and has repeatedly offered security guarantees. In the same briefing, according to secondary reports, she said NATO's strategic goal is war with Russia, citing the build-up on the eastern flank and Estonia's border closure.
corroboration: The first statement is from TASS; the second from a Turkish outlet citing CGTN, so it is secondhand.
analysis: The two lines are familiar Russian messaging. Lithuania's assessment warns that Russia could carry out limited operations against NATO in the longer term, so a denial of intent is not reassurance on its own.

title: Report: Swedish Gripen was cleared to shoot down the missile but held fire
summary: Rzeczpospolita, as reported by the Kyiv Post, says a Swedish Gripen pilot on NATO duty had clearance to shoot down the suspected Kh-101 over Poland but did not fire because of severe weather. Polish radars tracked 11 potential threats that night.
corroboration: Single report; not confirmed by Sweden, Poland or NATO in the sources found.
analysis: If confirmed, it would show that NATO's rules of engagement allowed a shoot-down but conditions did not. It would also echo the drone that NATO jets twice failed to bring down over Lithuania on 10–11 November.

title: Prosecutors: all three objects that entered Poland were Russian Kh-101 missiles
summary: On 22 November the Lublin District Prosecutor's Office said its preliminary findings show that all three objects that crossed into Poland on 20 November were Kh-101 cruise missiles, with debris at Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik and Mołodycz. It said the missiles were made in recent weeks at a plant in Dubna near Moscow. Work at the last site was due to finish on 23 November.
corroboration: Reported by Reuters (syndicated), the Kyiv Independent and others from the same prosecutors' statement, so this is one source. It replaces the defence ministry's first account of two missiles and a drone; one specialist outlet still cites doubt about the other two objects.
analysis: The finding strengthens the case that Russian missiles were involved but says nothing about intent. Missiles made weeks earlier and fired in a mass strike on Ukraine fit both a navigation error and deliberate routing; Poland has not published flight paths.

title: NATO ambassadors meet on Poland's security
summary: The North Atlantic Council holds an extraordinary meeting in Brussels on 23 November, announced by Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. Poland is expected to propose stronger air defence and surveillance on the eastern flank. Reports do not describe it as an Article 4 consultation.
corroboration: Announced by Polish officials and reported by several outlets; NATO's own readout was not yet available.
analysis: The meeting is a political and practical response (more air defence, more surveillance), not a step toward collective defence. Watch for new NATO deployments under the Eastern Sentry mission.

title: Sparta II towed out of Finnish waters; helicopter probe still open
summary: A Russian rescue vessel began towing the drone-damaged cargo ship Sparta II on 22 November, and by evening it had left Finland's economic zone; Finland lifted its sea and air restrictions and reported no leaks. Finland's defence ministry is still investigating a suspected Russian helicopter airspace violation of up to about 4 km off Loviisa on 21 November, which Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said was possibly linked to the rescue or monitoring.
corroboration: Finnish Border Guard and coast guard statements carried by Yle, Reuters and The Moscow Times. Officials still differ on where the ship was hit: Finland's Border Guard chief said Russian territorial waters, while Finnish defence officials and a Russian governor spoke of international waters near the border.
analysis: The quick hand-over limits the risk of a wider incident, but the Kaliningrad sea supply route now passes through a zone where the Russia–Ukraine war can reach. The helicopter case looks like a side effect of the rescue rather than a deliberate probe, pending the investigation.

title: Russian outlets blame NATO, Poland and Lithuania for Kaliningrad alert
summary: After Saturday evening's air alerts around Kaliningrad, Russian outlets and channels claimed that NATO attacked the region, that German troops in Poland coordinated a Ukrainian strike, or that Poland and Lithuania fired Ukrainian missiles. Poland's counter-disinformation centre called these claims false. Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys categorically rejected any role, and Lithuania's crisis centre said its air force detected no drones and that circulating fire photos came from Iran.
corroboration: Polish warning reported by RMF24 via UNN and by a Polish security consultancy; Lithuanian denials reported by TASS, Anadolu, Euromaidan Press and the Kyiv Post.
analysis: The accusations rest on the regional governor's remark about an object from the direction of Lithuania, for which no evidence has been shown. A consultancy expects such claims to peak around today's NATO meeting.

title: Strike on the Baltic Fleet base: footage real, hit unproven
summary: Ukrainian channels and some headlines described a first drone strike on the Baltic Fleet base at Baltiysk on 21 November. Analysts geolocated air-defence fire to the port area, but no damage or casualties have been verified, Ukraine has not claimed an attack and Russia's defence ministry did not list Kaliningrad among its overnight drone claims.
corroboration: Videos geolocated by OSINT analysts; one widely shared photo of a fire was traced to Qeshm Island, Iran. A fact-checking site rated the footage genuine and the strike claim unproven.
analysis: Air-defence fire shows something triggered a response; it does not show what was hit. Headlines saying drones struck the base go beyond the evidence.

title: Polish commander: Gripen had clearance but could not identify the missile
summary: Lt Gen Ireneusz Nowak, commander of Poland's Operational Command, told Rzeczpospolita that a Swedish Gripen under NATO command was cleared to engage but could not identify the Kh-101 visually or with sensors in very poor weather. Poland tracked 11 objects that night, three of which crossed the border; no one was hurt.
corroboration: Interview reported by Euromaidan Press and the Kyiv Independent; it confirms on the record what yesterday rested on press reporting.
analysis: The account explains the missed interception without suggesting a political decision not to fire. It raises the practical question NATO is discussing today: how to engage fast, low-flying missiles in bad weather.

title: Russia tells Estonia it is on the verge of triggering open war
summary: On 23 November Russia's foreign ministry summoned Estonia's chargé d'affaires in Moscow to protest Tallinn's decision to close its road crossings with Russia from 1 December for at least six months. The ministry called Estonia's accusation that Russian intelligence was behind an attempted arson at a drone maker unfounded, repeated that Estonia lets Ukrainian drones use its airspace, listed grievances over grain transit, shipping, language and the Orthodox Church, and said Tallinn's actions were bringing things to the brink of open war. It reserved political and diplomatic countermeasures. Estonia rejected the accusations and denied its territory is used for Ukrainian military operations.
corroboration: Reported by Reuters and AFP (via Al Jazeera and RTE), The Moscow Times, Meduza and Ukrainian outlets, all from the same ministry statement, so this is one source. Translations differ slightly on the exact wording.
analysis: This is an explicit warning aimed at a NATO member, but it is framed as a diplomatic protest and names no military step. It fits the baseline's picture of Russian pressure through rhetoric and information. The drone-airspace accusation has been made before without evidence; watch whether Moscow follows with concrete measures after 1 December.

title: NATO council meets on Poland; no outcome published
summary: The North Atlantic Council held its extraordinary meeting on Poland on 23 November. No statement or decision had been published by this morning. Secretary General Mark Rutte, speaking in Berlin, called the missile incursion dangerous and said it was for the authorities to establish whether it was deliberate. Poland's Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said allied early-warning aircraft were reinforcing Polish airspace.
corroboration: Based on an aggregation of several outlets and Notes from Poland. Accounts differ on whether the aircraft are already flying (Monday reports) or were still expected (the minister's 21 November post), and on when Rutte made his pledge to defend every inch of Polish territory.
analysis: Without a published outcome, the meeting's main signal is political solidarity and more surveillance, not a move toward collective defence. Prosecutors' finding of three Kh-101 missiles still stands; nothing new on intent.

title: Kaliningrad alert: analysis shows a small number of accounts drove the 'NATO attack' story
summary: A media-monitoring company that reviewed 2,875 publications in 31 languages found that 355 of 450 posts about a 'NATO attack' on Kaliningrad came from three accounts, and that Russian media spoke of an 'attack' mainly after Lithuania issued its denial. Lithuania's Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas called the episode a psychological operation; Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the authorities had information that Russia could use the incident to stage actions against Lithuania.
corroboration: Reported by LRT from the company's release and by BNS; the monitoring firm's method is not independently checked. Lithuania's crisis centre said its air force detected no drones.
analysis: The findings support the view that the accusations against Lithuania were amplified by a few sources rather than based on evidence. They also show a delay of over four hours in Lithuania's first public response, which let the narrative spread.

title: Four EU states plan joint team on Starlink arson attacks
summary: Prosecutors from Poland, Germany, Lithuania and Bulgaria plan a joint investigation team into arson attacks on Starlink infrastructure, including a fire at a ground station in Poland in September, a fire near Sofia in October and a foiled attempt in Vilnius. They are due to meet in early December. German authorities are to decide within two weeks whether to hand two suspects to Poland under European arrest warrants.
corroboration: Reported by LRT/BNS and Anadolu, both citing the Polish broadcaster RMF24; Polish ministers have blamed Russian intelligence.
analysis: A joint team suggests prosecutors see one network across four countries. The Russian link rests on Polish official statements; no court has ruled. These cases were already counted, so they do not change today's figures.

title: Russia funds rail ferries for Kaliningrad
summary: Russia's Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin announced funding of about $620 million for two rail ferries, to be built by 2030, on a route from Ust-Luga to Baltiysk. Ukrainian outlets present the plan as preparation for a blockade of Kaliningrad if transit through Lithuania is cut.
corroboration: Reported by United24 citing The Insider; no independent intelligence source. The same report notes that NATO has announced no blockade plan.
analysis: The ferries reduce Kaliningrad's dependence on rail transit through Lithuania, which matters for supply in a crisis, but they are years away. Headlines about a blockade go further than the evidence.

title: German tabloid: tanks sent to Lithuania by rail to avoid provoking Moscow
summary: Bild, citing unnamed sources, reported that German equipment for the Grand Eagle 26 exercise in Lithuania went by rail rather than by road through Poland to avoid provoking the Kremlin. Germany's defence ministry said changing the mode of transport is normal and must be practised. Germany plans a full brigade in Lithuania by the end of 2027.
corroboration: Single tabloid report relayed by Meduza; not confirmed elsewhere.
analysis: The motive rests on anonymous sources; the official explanation is routine logistics. Either way, moving heavy equipment by rail to Lithuania is itself an exercise of NATO reinforcement routes.

title: Ukrainian intelligence: Russia recruits saboteurs through job ads
summary: Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) said on 23 November that Russia has posted more than 20 million disguised job ads on Discord since January, plus messages on WhatsApp and Telegram, offering $1,500–3,000 to recruit young, vulnerable people, refugees and migrants for sabotage and data collection, particularly in the Baltic states.
corroboration: Reported by the Kyiv Post and United24 from HUR's statement; no independent confirmation of the figures.
analysis: Recruitment through online job offers matches the baseline's warning about hostile services recruiting Lithuanian citizens, but the scale given by HUR, a party to the war, cannot be checked.

title: Second Russian incursion into Poland; NATO sends an AWACS aircraft
summary: Shortly before midnight on 23 November, during a Russian attack on western Ukraine, a Russian drone crossed into Polish airspace. Poland's armed forces tracked it and authorised a shoot-down but held fire when it turned back toward Ukraine, citing risk to civilians. RMF24, citing unnamed sources, reported that it was jet-powered, flew about 20 km in and stayed for about nine minutes. After the North Atlantic Council met on 23 November, NATO's spokesperson said the Supreme Allied Commander Europe had authorised forward deployment of an AWACS aircraft and was examining further assets. Deputy Defence Minister Paweł Zalewski said Poland assumes the drone was sent on purpose and that no offensive measures are being considered.
corroboration: On-record statements from Poland's Operational Command, Deputy Defence Minister Zalewski and NATO's spokesperson, reported by Notes from Poland, European Pravda, Militarnyi and Fox News. The drone's speed, depth and duration come from RMF24's unnamed sources only. Reports differ on whether the drone came on Monday night or overnight into Tuesday; this is the same event.
analysis: Two Russian incursions in four days push Poland's case for stronger air defence, but NATO's reply so far is surveillance, not escalation. Poland's claim of intent is an assessment; Russia has not commented.

title: Polish commander: NATO pilot was cleared to fire on 20 November but held off
summary: Poland's Operational Commander, Lt. Gen. Ireneusz Nowak, said a Swedish Gripen on NATO air policing had conditional clearance from NATO's air operations centre to shoot down one of the missiles on 20 November, but the pilot could not identify the target in very bad weather. Separately, Poland's chargé d'affaires in Washington said he briefed the US National Security Council and renewed Warsaw's call for permanent US troops in Poland.
corroboration: The clearance rests on the Polish commander's account, first reported by Rzeczpospolita and repeated by the Kyiv Post and Fox News; NATO has not confirmed it on the record. Sweden's armed forces said only that their jets tracked several unidentified objects.
analysis: If confirmed, it shows NATO was ready to engage a Russian missile over allied territory, a meaningful step. It also shows the limits of air policing in poor weather, which helps explain Poland's push for more allied air defence and US troops.

title: Sweden warns of GPS jamming around Stockholm
summary: Flight-tracking data showed the share of aircraft near Stockholm-Arlanda with GPS interference rising from about 1% to 40–50% between 21 and 23 November. Swedish aviation authorities issued a notice to pilots warning of possible jamming and spoofing within about 95 nautical miles of Stockholm, valid until 31 December. Sweden's Transport Agency said it did not know the source, had ruled out space weather, and that air traffic had not been affected.
corroboration: The official notice and Transport Agency comments were reported by Dagens Nyheter (via an aggregator) and the Cypriot outlet Sigmalive; the 40–50% figure comes from open flight data and a social-media post. An incident tracker also listed it.
analysis: Interference this far west is unusual. Russia has been blamed for persistent jamming in the eastern Baltic, but one analyst quoted in the coverage doubted this pattern could come from Russian territory; attribution is open.

title: Estonia's prime minister: border closure is in substance indefinite
summary: In an ERR interview on 24 November, Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the closure of all four road crossings with Russia from 1 December is officially temporary with a review after six months, but in substance indefinite, because he does not expect the threat to ease. He said closing the Narva rail crossing remains a possible next step if needed and that responses to Russia need not be symmetrical. He said Estonia has been targeted 12 times by incidents attributable to Russia.
corroboration: Single on-record interview with ERR. Earlier, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the closure would backfire, and the foreign ministry protested on 23 November.
analysis: Tallinn is signalling that it will not reverse course under Russian pressure. Rail freight continues for now, so the economic link is not fully cut.

title: Lithuanian officials differ on what the Kaliningrad alert meant
summary: Deividas Matulionis, President Gitanas Nausėda's chief national security adviser, said on 24 November that the 21 November Kaliningrad alert more likely reflected Moscow's fear of a Ukrainian attack than an attempt to provoke NATO, warned that escalation would only give Russia a pretext, and said Lithuania has no plans to restrict access to Kaliningrad. A day earlier Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas had called the Russian reports and officials' actions an attempt to provoke Lithuania.
corroboration: Reported by LRT from BNS. Kaliningrad's governor said a suspicious object from the Lithuanian side triggered the alert; an inspection found no threat.
analysis: The two readings are not incompatible, but the difference matters: one stresses Russian intent to provoke, the other Russian nervousness. Neither suggests a military build-up.

title: Polish officials track false stories about the missile incursion
summary: A commercial security firm's weekly assessment, citing Poland's digital affairs minister and state counter-disinformation centre, lists false stories that spread after 20 November: that one object was a Ukrainian drone, that Polish services planted the debris, that Ukraine let the missiles through to drag Poland into the war, and that the government would use the incident to cancel elections. The minister put views at around 20 million and attributed most to Russian and Belarusian sources.
corroboration: Single commercial summary of Polish official statements; primary sources not linked. Prosecutors' identification of Kh-101 debris contradicts the main claims.
analysis: Fits the baseline's warning about information operations accompanying physical incidents. The view count and attribution are the government's figures and are not independently checked.

title: Finnish lawmakers back anti-tank barriers on the Russian border
summary: Heikki Autto, chair of the Finnish parliament's defence committee, said anti-tank barriers should be built along the Russian border in peacetime, drawing on Ukraine's experience; an opposition Social Democrat member backed the idea and called it an alliance matter. Finland finished a 200 km border fence in September.
corroboration: Bloomberg report relayed by Meduza; no government decision yet.
analysis: A long-term defensive measure that reflects how front-line states expect a lasting confrontation, consistent with the baseline; it is not a reaction to a specific new threat.

title: Poland plans a no-fly zone along its eastern border
summary: Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk said on 25 November that the ministry will ask the government for a no-fly zone 12 to a few dozen kilometres deep along the eastern border, with a regulation to be processed in the coming weeks and in force possibly by early January. It follows three Russian cruise missiles that came down in south-eastern Poland on 20 November and a Russian drone that entered Polish airspace on the night of 23–24 November. Bloomberg, citing unnamed sources, reported that Poland raised the idea of downing missiles over Ukraine at NATO; Tomczyk could not confirm this and said NATO opposes it.
corroboration: Notes from Poland, TVP World and ABC/WEIS report the minister's announcement; the NATO discussion rests on Bloomberg's unnamed sources only.
analysis: A defensive, procedural step that makes interception easier on Poland's own territory. The more escalatory idea, shooting over Ukraine, is unconfirmed and, by Poland's own account, opposed by NATO. The opposition calls the plan cosmetic.

title: Lithuania detains five over suspected paid work for Russian state media
summary: Lithuanian prosecutors said on 25 November that five people were detained on suspicion of assisting another state against Lithuania, allegedly collecting information and producing content for Russian state broadcaster RTRS for payment since autumn 2024. More than ten searches were carried out with the intelligence services. Media link the probe to a group that flooded state institutions with requests.
corroboration: LRT/BNS from the Prosecutor General's Office; no independent detail yet.
analysis: Fits the baseline's warning about Russian information operations and recruitment of Lithuanian citizens. These are suspicions, not convictions, and the suspects are not named here.

title: Lithuanian man charged with spying on aid to Ukraine
summary: The Kaunas regional prosecutor's office said on 25 November it has sent to court the case of a Lithuanian man accused of gathering intelligence for Russia on strategic infrastructure and aid to Ukraine since August 2021, and of illegally holding firearms, ammunition and explosives. The case began after a March 2025 incident in which he allegedly photographed Ukraine aid at a private company and used tear gas on an employee who confronted him.
corroboration: LRT/BNS from prosecutors.
analysis: Another example of the recruitment pattern described in the Lithuanian threat assessment. It is an indictment, not a verdict; we count it as espionage, not sabotage.

title: Latvia's prime minister: Estonia closed its Russia border in haste
summary: Latvia's prime minister told TV3 that Estonia should have consulted the other Baltic states before deciding to close its road crossings with Russia from 1 December, and suggested the timing reflected Estonia's spring elections; Riga was due to decide on its own possible closure on 26 November.
